Hand Injuries

Slide 1

Plastic Surgery – 453 Surg Course

Slide 2

Median Nerve – Carpal Tunnel Syndrome

  • Signs and symptoms:
    • Numbness in the radial 3 ½ digits
    • More at night, with excessive use
    • Wasting in the thenar muscles
    • Weak thumb abduction
  • Special Manruvers:
    • Phalen’s
    • Tinel’s
  • Investigation
    • Nerve conduction study (NCS)
  • Treatment:
    • Lifestyle modification
    • Splint at night
    • Surgery (carpal tunnel release)
Notes

Clinical picture

SYMPTOMS

Numbness in the radial 3½ digits: thumb, index, middle and the radial half of the ring finger
Worse at night
Worse with sustained use: holding a phone, driving, hands kept raised
Drops things because they can't feel them. CTS patients complain of this more than anyone

SIGNS

Thenar wasting (the nerve mainly supplies the thenar muscles)
Weak thumb abduction: can't lift the thumb away from the palm
Progressive: gets worse with time
  • Numbness of thumb, index and middle fingers, weak thumb opposition, positive Tinel's → carpal tunnel syndrome. 441
  • Root supplying middle finger sensation → C7. 438 ×2
Notes

Confirming the diagnosis

TestHowPositive result
Tinel's signTap over the median nerve at the carpal tunnelElectric tingling shooting into the median distribution. A healthy, non-irritated nerve gives nothing
Phalen's testHold the wrist in full flexion (reverse Phalen's: full extension). Bending the nerve like a wire further cuts its conductionSymptoms within 30–60 seconds. A normal person can hold it for ~10 minutes without symptoms
Nerve conduction study Treatment ladderStimulate the median nerve across the wrist and measure conduction speedSpeed below the normal reference or the other hand confirms compression
1 Lifestyle Keyboard wrist rest and gel mouse pad keep the wrist neutral, not extended. Regular breaks, stretching. Common in manual and computer workers.·2 Night splint Sleeping with the wrist bent or lying on the hand adds external pressure on top of the internal pressure. The splint stops that.·3 Steroid injection Used by some surgeons. Can reduce swelling inside the tunnel, but it is not a cure.·4 Carpal tunnel decompression The only definitive treatment.
Splint rules
A splint controls symptoms; it does not treat the compression. Judge it after a 3-week trial. If lifestyle changes plus splinting don't settle the symptoms, the answer is surgery.
Compression never resolves by itself
Once it starts it only stabilises or gets worse. Not everyone needs surgery: symptoms that come and go and settle with rest can be managed conservatively. Constant, persistent symptoms → decompression.
The cable analogy
Rest a heavy table on a cable for two or three hours and it recovers. Leave it for two weeks and part of it is permanently damaged. A nerve under prolonged compression may not come back.
Goals of surgery, and what to tell the patient
(1) Prevent further deterioration and (2) give the nerve a chance to recover. In very chronic, severe cases (e.g. numb for seven years) recovery may be incomplete. Manage expectations before operating.
Added explanationWhen a hand fracture is splinted, use the safe ("intrinsic-plus") position: wrist ~30° extension, MCP joints 60–90° flexion, IP joints straight — the collateral ligaments stay at full length, so the joints don't stiffen.
  • Metacarpal shaft fracture treated conservatively — splint position → PIP neutral, MCP 60° flexion, wrist 30° extension. 437
Notes

Ulnar Nerve: Cubital Tunnel Syndrome

The same story as the median nerve, but the squeeze is at the elbow instead of the wrist.

Notes

Nerve Laceration: Repair or Transfer

A cut nerve gives the same numbness and weakness as compression, but immediately. Wasting comes later.

Injury

3 months

6 months and later

Tendon transfer after 6 months
Nerve repair within the first 6 months

Median or ulnar laceration

Observe, manage conservatively·No recovery: explore and repair·No recovery: tendon transfer

Radial palsy after humeral

fracture

Why the 6-month cut-off
With compression, signals still reach the muscle, so it stays responsive. After a cut, the muscle gets no stimulation. After more than 6 months its "receiver" stops working: the muscle is alive but will not contract, however well the nerve is repaired.
Tendon transfer
Move a working muscle's tendon to take over the lost action, for example restoring thumb abduction after a median nerve injury. You give up one function to regain another.
  • After shoulder reduction: lost sensation over the lateral arm and arm abduction → axillary nerve. 438 ×6
  • Weak shoulder abduction, numb lateral arm, weak biceps reflex → C5. 434 ×2
Notes

Hand Fractures: General Approach

More of an orthopaedic topic. Know how to describe a fracture, how treatment steps up, and the four words that mean surgery.

Slide 3

Ulnar Nerve – Cubital Tunnel Syndrome

  • Signs and symptoms:
    • Numbness in the ulnar 1 ½ digits
    • Weakness and difficulty with fine movement
    • Wasting in the first web space
    • Weak finger adduction/abduction,
    • Claw hand
  • Special Manoeuvres:
    • Tinel’s
    • Froment test
  • Investigation
    • Nerve conduction study (NCS)
  • Treatment:
    • Lifestyle modification
    • Splint at night
    • Surgery (cubital tunnel release)
Notes

Who supplies what, and how a nerve fails

CompressionLaceration (cut nerve)
OnsetGradual; comes and goes, then persistsImmediate, at the moment of injury
Numbness and weaknessBuild up; worse at night and with usePresent from day one
WastingAppears as compression becomes chronicDelayed: develops over the following months
The muscleStill receives signal, so it stays responsiveNo signal; stops responding after ~6 months
TreatmentConservative trial, then surgical decompressionUnder 6 months: nerve repair Over 6 months: tendon transfer
Notes

Median Nerve: Carpal Tunnel Syndrome

The most common nerve compression in the hand.

Why the nerve gets squeezed
Floor of the tunnel = carpal bones (hard). Roof = transverse carpal ligament (hard). Between them run the median nerve and the flexor tendons. Nothing can expand, so any extra pressure (a sustained wrist position, sleeping on the hand) lands straight on the nerve.
Added explanationGanglion — the commonest hand/wrist lump, typically on the dorsum of the wrist: smooth, firm to hard (tense), fixed to the joint capsule/tendon sheath, may vary in size and transilluminate; young adults, often women.
Notes

Clinical picture

SYMPTOMS

Numbness in the ulnar 1½ digits: little finger and the ulnar half of the ring finger
Loss of fine movements: writing, doing their hair, fastening a necklace. The ulnar nerve runs the fine-movement muscles

SIGNS

Wasting of the first dorsal interosseous (first web space), not the thenar eminence
Claw hand
Weak finger abduction and adduction (interossei)
Tinel's at the elbow: tapping the cubital tunnel sends tingling into the ulnar fingers
Median vs ulnar: listen to the complaint
Carpal tunnel patient: "I keep dropping things" (sensory loss). Cubital tunnel patient: "I can't do fine tasks" (weak intrinsic muscles).
  • Claw hand after K-wire insertion at the elbow → ulnar nerve. 438 ×4
  • Patient can't make the "OK" sign → anterior interosseous nerve. 439 ×5
Notes

Froment's test

Classic ulnar triad
Claw hand + wasting of the first dorsal interosseous + positive Froment's test. Confirm with a nerve conduction study.
  • Same scenario with both thumb abduction and opposition offered → thumb opposition (completely lost; abduction partly kept by abductor pollicis longus). 437 ×4
Added explanationFDP inserts on the distal phalanx and is the only flexor of the DIP joint; FDS flexes the PIP. A cut over the middle phalanx/DIP that stops DIP flexion = FDP. Test FDP by holding the PIP straight and asking the patient to bend the fingertip.
  • Laceration at the DIP level (picture), can't flex the fingertip → flexor digitorum profundus. 437
Added explanationFlexor (septic) tenosynovitis — after a penetrating injury: Kanavel's signs — finger held flexed, fusiform swelling, tenderness along the tendon sheath, severe pain on passive extension → IV antibiotics and urgent surgical drainage/washout of the sheath. A felon is a pulp-space abscess of the fingertip.
Notes

Treatment ladder

1 Lifestyle Stop leaning on the elbows: hard desks, unpadded chair arms, studying in bed propped on the elbows. Classic in students during exam season and after lots of writing.·2 Night splint Most people sleep with the elbows bent, which presses on the nerve. A towel wrapped around the elbow at night keeps it straight.·3 Surgical decompression If lifestyle changes and splinting both fail.
Ulnar laceration
Numbness, weakness and clawing appear immediately; wasting is delayed. Same treatment as the median nerve: acute → nerve repair, late → tendon transfer.
Exam pattern
A median or ulnar nerve scenario in the exam is almost always the tunnel (compression), not a laceration.
Notes

Three Nerves Side by Side

MedianUlnarRadial
Compression siteCarpal tunnel (wrist)Cubital tunnel (elbow)Radial tunnel (forearm)
Sensory lossRadial 3½ digitsUlnar 1½ digitsSmall dorsal patch, rarely noticed
Key motor lossThumb abduction (thenar)Finger abduction and adduction; fine movementsWrist, finger and thumb extension
WastingThenar eminenceFirst dorsal interosseous—
Deformity—Claw handWrist drop
Patient says"I drop things"; worse at night"I can't write or do my hair""My hand falls"
Special testsTinel's (wrist), Phalen'sTinel's (elbow), Froment'sNerve conduction study
Typical causeCompressionCompressionTrauma: humeral shaft fracture
SurgeryCarpal tunnel decompressionCubital tunnel decompressionRadial tunnel release; nerve repair or tendon transfer after trauma
  • Complete median nerve transection at the wrist — expected loss → abduction of the thumb. 432 ×2
  • Radial head fracture, can't extend the digits but can extend the wrist and elbow, no sensory loss → posterior interosseous nerve. 438 ×2
  • Fall on an outstretched hand, fracture near the snuffbox → scaphoid. 436
Added explanationDermatomes and roots: C5 lateral arm (deltoid, shoulder abduction, biceps reflex) · C6 lateral forearm and thumb · C7 middle finger · C8 little finger · T1 medial forearm. Erb's palsy (C5–C6, birth injury) → "waiter's tip" posture: arm adducted and internally rotated, elbow extended, forearm pronated. Klumpke's (C8–T1) → claw hand.
  • C5–C6 root injury — sensory loss → lateral aspect of the arm and forearm. 437
Slide 4

Radial Nerve (Radial Tunnel Syndrome - Post. Interossious Nerve)

  • Signs and symptoms:
    • Pain and weakness in wrist and finger extension without sensory involvement
  • Investigation
    • Nerve conduction study (NCS)
  • Treatment:
    • Surgery (cubital tunnel release)
  • Needle prick, then flexed swollen finger with severe pain on passive extension → septic tenosynovitis. 436
Added explanationHigh-voltage electrical injury — small skin burns hide extensive deep muscle necrosis → compartment syndrome (pain on passive stretch) even with palpable pulses → fasciotomy. Escharotomy releases only a constricting circumferential skin eschar.
  • Electrical injury, burns at the flexor creases, palmar pulses present, pain on passive finger motion → fasciotomy. 435 ×3
  • 24-year-old woman, smooth hard immobile 2 × 2 cm mass on the dorsum of the hand, pain on wrist flexion → ganglion. 435 ×3
Notes

Radial Nerve: Tunnel Syndrome and Fracture Palsy

Mostly a motor nerve, and unlike the median nerve, its problems usually come from injury rather than compression.

WHAT IT DOESWHEN IT'S COMPRESSED
• Extends the wrist, fingers and thumb• Radial tunnel syndrome, also called posterior interosseous
• Sensation to only a small patch on the back of the hand; mostnerve (PIN) syndrome
patients never notice its loss• The hand drops (wrist drop, per the lecture) • Confirm with NCS; treat with radial tunnel release
Textbook nuance worth knowing
The PIN branches off after the nerve to extensor carpi radialis longus, so pure PIN compression classically gives finger and thumb drop with wrist extension preserved (the wrist deviates radially). A full wrist drop points to a higher lesion, such as the spiral groove. The lecture groups these together; know the distinction in case it is tested.
  • Humerus fracture, can't extend the fingers or wrist → radial nerve. 439 ×7
Added explanationAnterior interosseous nerve (branch of the median) — pure motor to FPL, FDP of index/middle and pronator quadratus → can't make the "OK" sign (pinches with straight thumb IP and index DIP), no sensory loss. Axillary nerve (shoulder dislocation/reduction) → loss of deltoid abduction and the "regimental badge" patch over the lateral upper arm.
Notes

The usual story: humeral shaft fracture

The radial nerve wraps around the humerus in the spiral groove, so it gets injured by the fracture itself or during orthopaedic fixation. The key history question: when did the wrist drop start?

At the moment of injury The nerve was most likely stretched or bruised (neurapraxia). Being cut by the fracture alone is very unlikely, so it is expected to recover.Only after reduction or surgery The nerve may be trapped (between fragments or under hardware) or cut. Much more concerning, with a lower threshold to explore.
Management after a humeral fracture
Most are managed conservatively for the first 3 months. No recovery by 3 months → nerve exploration and repair. No recovery by 6 months → tendon transfer.
Slide 5

Hand Fractures

  • Classification/Description:
    • Open vs Closed
    • Spiral / Oblique vs Transverse
    • Simple vs Comminuted
    • Extra vs intra articular
    • Displaced vs non-displaced
Notes

The Big Picture

Added explanationScaphoid — the commonest carpal fracture: fall on an outstretched hand with anatomical snuffbox tenderness; may not show on the first X-ray → immobilize and re-image (or MRI); risk of avascular necrosis of the proximal pole.
Notes

Describe the fracture

FeatureOptions
SkinOpen (communicates with a wound) or closed
PatternTransverse, oblique or spiral
FragmentsSimple (two pieces) or comminuted (more than two pieces)
JointExtra-articular or intra-articular (fracture line enters the joint)
PositionDisplaced or undisplaced
Management ladderA precise description tells the next doctor what needs to be done.
1 Immobilisation Cast or splint. The simplest option, for fractures in an acceptable position.·2 Closed reduction + immobilisation For a displaced fracture: manipulate it back into place without opening the skin, then immobilise.·3 Operative fixation Closed (reduce, then fix through the skin) or open reduction and internal fixation (ORIF).
Cast vs splint
Cast = can't be removed. Splint = removable. In the emergency department, apply a cast so the patient can't take it off before the specialist sees them (usually within a week). A fracture that could have healed in plaster may displace and need surgery if the patient removes a splint.
Is the position acceptable?
Check that the fingers stay parallel with the hand open and closed. If they do, a cast is fine even when the X-ray isn't perfect. The goal is a normal X-ray and normal function, and function wins.
Slide 6

Management

  • Immobilization: (splinting / cast)
  • Closed reduction and Immobilization
  • Operative fixation:
    • Closed reduction and internal fixation
    • Open reduction and internal fixation (ORIF)
Notes

Fixation: K-wires vs plates and screws

K-wiresPlates and screws
TechniqueClosed: reduce, check on X-ray, drill a smooth wire across the fractureOpen: expose the fracture and reduce it under direct vision, so the reduction is better
InvasivenessLess invasive, no scarLeaves a scar
HardwareNone left inside: wires stick out through the skin and are pulled out at ~6 weeksStays in; designed to be permanent. Removal needs a second operation, not before ~6 months, usually only if it bothers the patient
StabilityLess rigid: some movement possible, no compressionStrong, anatomical fixation
RehabilitationMovement waits until the wires are outEarlier mobilisation and therapy
Final result
Same healing in the end. The difference is speed of recovery and stability.
Choosing between them
Depends on the fracture (some are too small or fragmented for screws, others for wires) and on the patient: someone who doesn't want hardware can try K-wires, converting to screws if needed.
  • Open fracture of the 4th and 5th metacarpals → external fixation and K-wires (operative). 437
Slide 7

Indication for Operative Management

  • Multiple finger fractures
  • Rotation / scissoring
  • Instability
  • Comminuted fractures
Notes

When to operate

Any one of these four means operative fixation
Multiple finger fractures
A sign of severe trauma. A broken finger normally leans on its intact neighbours for support; when they are broken too, nothing holds it.
Rotation / scissoring
Fingers should stay parallel. A rotated fracture makes the finger cross over its neighbour when the patient makes a fist.
Instability
The fracture slips back out of position after it has been reduced.
Comminuted fracture
Several fragments that a cast cannot hold in place.
Exam strategy
Fracture scenarios turn on these four words. If any of them appears, pick the operation option. Only one operative option is offered: you won't be asked to choose open vs closed, because that is decided in theatre.
  • Closed 5th metacarpal fracture with scissoring of the 4th and 5th digits → call the hand surgeon and book the OR. 437

Median → carpal tunnel (wrist). Ulnar → cubital tunnel (elbow). Radial → mostly trauma (humeral shaft fracture, spiral groove).

Sensory: median = radial 3½ digits; ulnar = ulnar 1½ digits; radial = small dorsal patch, rarely noticed.

Wasting: thenar eminence (median) vs first dorsal interosseous / first web space (ulnar).

Complaints: carpal tunnel drops things and is worse at night; cubital tunnel loses fine movements (writing, hair, necklace).

Tests: Tinel's + Phalen's for carpal tunnel (positive within 30–60 s); Tinel's at the elbow + Froment's (thumb IP bends) for ulnar; NCS confirms every compression.

A splint controls symptoms; it doesn't cure. Give it a 3-week trial. Surgery is the only definitive treatment because compression only stabilises or worsens.

Chronic, severe compression may not fully recover after decompression, so manage expectations.

Cut nerve: symptoms immediate, wasting delayed. Under 6 months → nerve repair; over 6 months → tendon transfer.

Radial palsy after a humeral fracture: ask when the wrist drop started. Observe 3 months → explore and repair → tendon transfer at 6 months.

Operate on a hand fracture if there are multiple fractures, rotation/scissoring, instability or comminution. In the ED, apply a cast, not a removable splint.

K-wires: less invasive, out at 6 weeks, less rigid. Plates and screws: rigid, anatomical, faster rehab, but a scar and permanent hardware. Same final healing.

  • Newborn with a "waiter's tip" posture → Erb's palsy. 429
